title: Why boarding back to front is the slow way
description:
Back-to-front boarding puts everyone in one line behind whoever is lifting a bag: 72 passengers, 71 waits. In a 2011 test on a 12-row cabin set, strict back to front took 6:11, letting people on at random 4:44, and the Steffen method (window seats two rows apart, 12F, 10F, 8F..., then the other rows, then middles and aisles) 3:36, because six people stow bags at the same time without blocking each other.

Numbers checked in code: the measured times from the paper and a simple aisle simulation (104,000 simulated boardings) that gives the same ranking. Source: Steffen & Hotchkiss, Experimental test of airplane boarding methods, arxiv.org/abs/1108.5211.

social_caption: Back-to-front boarding is slower than letting everyone on at random. Here's the order that's almost twice as fast.
facts_checked: Steffen & Hotchkiss tested boarding with 72 passengers on a mock 12-row cabin with six seats per row and one central aisle; Table 1 official times: back-front 6:11, blocks 6:54, Wilma 4:13, Steffen 3:36, random 4:44 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1108.5211, read via ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1108.5211)

Their back-to-front order went back row window, middle, aisle, then the next row forward; 'back-to-front boarding has no seat interferences, but it does have 71 aisle interferences' (https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1108.5211)
Steffen method: each passenger in line sits two rows from the one before, e.g. 12F, 10F, 8F, 6F, 4F, 2F, so neighbours can stow luggage at the same time (https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1108.5211)
6:11 - 4:44 = 87 s; 3:36 is 42% faster than 6:11; aisle simulation over 104,000 boardings: back-front 1.00, random 0.77 (measured 0.77), Wilma 0.61, Steffen 0.50; CTA 30F -> 28F (verify.py)

beats.say: Board your plane back to front, or at random? Random wins.
Back to front sounds smart: nobody walks past anyone. It's slower than chaos.
Your plane: 72 people, 12 rows, one aisle. A physicist timed each order on a cabin set.
Back to front: row 12 stops to lift a bag. Everyone behind them waits. 71 waits, in one line. 6 minutes 11.
Board at random, and rows 12, 3 and 8 lift their bags at the same time. 4 minutes 44.
But random is luck. Do it on purpose.
Line people up two rows apart: 12 window, 10 window, 8 window. Six bags go up at once, and nobody is in anyone's way.
Then the other windows, then middles, then aisles.
3 minutes 36. The order was never the problem. It's how many bags go up at once.
Your plane has 30 rows. Who boards right after 30F?
